content.content:
1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	When we say ``Model B outperforms Model A on MMLU,'' we implicitly assume that the benchmark measures the same construct in the same way for both models. This assumption of temporal comparability underpins every cross-generation comparison published on leaderboards and in model reports, yet it is rarely tested. Applying Mantel-Haenszel Differential Item Functioning (MH-DIF) analysis~\citep{holland1988mh} with Educational Testing Service (ETS) severity classification to the METABENCH response matrix~\citep{kipnis2024metabench}, we find that 31\% of MMLU~\citep{hendrycks2021mmlu} items receive ETS Category~C classification ($|\Delta_{\mathrm{MH}}| \geq 1.5$, $p < 0.05$), indicating large shifts in item functioning between models released in 2023 and 2024. This is not statistical noise: a random-split control within the 2023 cohort yields only 0.18\% ETS~C items. The instability persists within every MMLU subject domain, with domain-level C\% ranging from 31\% to 45\% (mean 38.1\%), and item-level regression shows that 92.4\% of this instability is unrelated to aggregate domain-level accuracy gains. Nearly one in three MMLU items behaves differently depending on when the evaluated models were trained.
5	
6	A growing body of contamination detection research has produced sophisticated item-level methods, from membership inference approaches such as Min-K\%~\citep{shi2024mink} to performance-based detectors such as ConStat~\citep{dekoninck2024constat}, DVD~\citep{liang2026dvd}, and Self-Critique~\citep{tao2026selfcritique}. These methods validate detection accuracy primarily against web-overlap labels such as those of \citet{li2024contamination}, which classify benchmark items as contaminated based on verbatim or near-verbatim matches in publicly accessible training corpora. Such labels measure \emph{global exposure}: whether an item exists in the data ecosystem that all training pipelines can access. They do not measure \emph{differential item functioning}: whether an item behaves differently across model cohorts that may have had varying degrees of exposure or different training methodologies. \Cref{fig:global_vs_differential} illustrates the distinction. Most MMLU items are globally contaminated in the sense that they exist in web-accessible text, so all model cohorts encounter them and no differential signal arises. The items that function differentially are those where exposure or training methodology changed asymmetrically across cohorts. Validating differential detectors against global-exposure labels therefore conflates two phenomena, and the near-chance enrichment (0.96) between DIF flags and web-overlap labels is the expected outcome of this mismatch.
7	
8	\begin{figure}[t]
9	\centering
10	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_1_global_vs_differential.pdf}
11	\caption{Global vs.\ differential contamination, illustrated via Item Characteristic Curves (ICCs). \textbf{Left}: global contamination produces no DIF; both cohorts encounter the item, and their ICCs overlap. \textbf{Right}: differential contamination produces DIF; the focal cohort's ICC shifts because only that cohort was disproportionately exposed during training. The enrichment ratio of $\approx 1.0$ between DIF flags and web-overlap labels is expected because most MMLU items fall into the left category.}
12	\label{fig:global_vs_differential}
13	\end{figure}
14	
15	We apply classical MH-DIF with ETS classification to the full METABENCH response matrix (5,227 models $\times$ 12,508 MMLU items), the largest-scale DIF analysis on LLM benchmarks to date. This psychometric approach is motivated by recent findings that contamination detectors are fragile under post-training~\citep{wang2026fragility} and by concurrent work using anchor-item calibration for score comparability~\citep{habba2026growingpains}, which addresses a complementary question (equating scores across cohorts) to ours (characterizing temporal item stability). We initially hypothesized that DIF could identify differentially contaminated items: benchmark questions whose statistical properties shifted because newer models had been trained on them. Semi-synthetic injection experiments confirmed detection capability ($\Delta\mathrm{TPR} = {+}0.508$ at exploitation rate $p = 0.5$), and our cross-subject matching protocol eliminated false positive inflation ($\Delta\mathrm{FPR} = 0.000$). Three structural refinements (matched-ability quintile analysis, IRT $\theta$-conditioning, and within-subject bifactor pre-checks) all failed to reduce the temporal C\% below 31\%, however. The persistent non-reduction shifted our research question: from whether DIF detects contamination, to what the persistent 31\% instability reveals about how benchmarks interact with evolving model populations.
16	
17	A natural tension arises between our headline finding and its practical consequences. On one hand, 31\% of items are functionally unstable across model generations. On the other, Spearman rank correlation between model rankings computed on all 12,508 items versus stable-only items is $\rho \approx 0.997$. The resolution lies in measurement redundancy: MMLU's 12,508 items provide sufficient statistical mass that removing nearly a third does not alter rank order. This is precisely why DIF should be understood as a diagnostic lens (which items changed and for which model families) rather than a quality filter (remove bad items to improve the benchmark). Despite aggregate stability, DIF-flagged items concentrate discriminative signal that differentiates model generations: removing DIF items degrades ranking discriminability more than removing an equal number of random items ($z = -8$ to $-49\sigma$ across 21 conditions). Individual model families show distinctive DIF profiles: Phi-3 and Llama-3 gain ${+}700$ to ${+}850$ rank positions under stable-item evaluation, while Mistral-based merges lose $-400$ to $-587$ positions.
18	
19	We do not modify the MH-DIF procedure itself. The contributions of this work lie in applying it at a scale and in a context where its standard assumptions face new challenges, and in the empirical findings that emerge. At 5,227 models, the analysis exceeds typical educational testing applications by orders of magnitude and requires careful attention to stratification and matching. Cross-subject matching, a protocol we introduce for semi-synthetic evaluation on multi-subject benchmarks, eliminates false positive inflation entirely ($\Delta\mathrm{FPR} = 0.000$). The ground truth analysis exposes a fundamental validation methodology gap: web-overlap labels cannot serve as ground truth for item-level differential detectors because global exposure and differential functioning are distinct phenomena. Cross-benchmark replication on GSM8K with independent contamination validation through the GSM1K held-out set~\citep{zhang2024gsm1k} confirms that the findings generalize beyond MMLU. We make the following contributions:
20	
21	\begin{enumerate}
22	\item \textbf{Benchmark temporal comparability} (Claim 1): 31\% of MMLU items are functionally unstable across model generations under ETS~C classification, with the instability persisting within every subject domain (mean C\% $= 38.1\%$) and confirmed non-random by random-split control at 0.18\% (\Cref{sec:temporal}).
23	
24	\item \textbf{Ground truth meta-critique} (Claim 2): Web-overlap contamination labels~\citep{li2024contamination} cannot evaluate item-level differential detectors. The enrichment between DIF flags and web-overlap labels is 0.96 (chance level), exposing a validation methodology gap in the contamination detection literature (\Cref{sec:groundtruth}).
25	
26	\item \textbf{Semi-synthetic validation framework} (Claim 3): Controlled injection with cross-subject matching achieves $\Delta\mathrm{FPR} = 0.000$ while preserving detection power ($\Delta\mathrm{TPR} = {+}0.508$ at $p = 0.5$); cross-benchmark replication on GSM8K confirms generality (\Cref{sec:semisynthetic,sec:gsm8k}).
27	
28	\item \textbf{DIF as diagnostic lens} (Claim 4): DIF-flagged items concentrate discriminative information ($z = -8$ to $-49\sigma$ vs.\ random removal) and anti-correlate with the GSM1K contamination gap ($r = -0.478$, suggestive at $N = 33$), indicating that DIF captures item-level behavioral change distinct from simple memorization (\Cref{sec:downstream,sec:gsm8k}).
29	\end{enumerate}
30

value.aiTitle: Paper framing for LLM benchmark psychometrics

content.content:
1	meta:
2	  venue: ICLR 2027
3	  track: main
4	  template: ""
5	  template_note: "ICLR 2027 template not yet available locally; will download or reuse iclr2025 when entering Step 2"
6	  page_limit: 9
7	  deadline: "2026-10-01"
8	  core_claim: >-
9	    Applying DIF to MMLU (5,227 models × 12,508 items) reveals 38% item-level
10	    functional instability across model generations, exposes a fundamental gap
11	    in contamination ground truth labels, and provides a semi-synthetic
12	    validation framework for item-level detectors.
13	  created_at: "2026-05-20T23:45:00Z"
14	  story_arc:
15	    hook: >-
16	      When we say "Model B outperforms Model A on MMLU," we assume temporal
17	      comparability — but 38% of MMLU items function differently across model
18	      generations.
19	    gap: >-
20	      Existing contamination labels (web-overlap, n-gram) measure global
21	      exposure, not differential item functioning — every validation study
22	      using these labels has a blind spot. This is a fundamental validation
23	      methodology gap affecting the entire contamination detection field.
24	    insight: >-
25	      DIF detects differential contamination (semi-synthetic ΔTPR=+0.508) but
26	      temporal DIF is dominated by genuine capability evolution
27	      (enrichment≈1.0, within-subject C%=38.1%), and three structural
28	      corrections cannot separate them.
29	    mechanism: >-
30	      Semi-synthetic injection into real response matrices provides controlled
31	      ground truth; cross-subject matching eliminates FPR inflation (ΔFPR=0.000).
32	    evidence: >-
33	      38% items functionally unstable (plan_001/014); ΔTPR=+0.508 at p=0.5
34	      (plan_011); ΔFPR=0.000 cross-subject (plan_016); three improvements
35	      exhausted (plan_001b/012/014).
36	
37	paper_outline:
38	  - section: abstract
39	    word_budget: 200
40	    core_bullets:
41	      - >-
42	        Problem: LLM benchmark scores assume temporal comparability, but
43	        item-level behavior may drift across model generations
44	      - >-
45	        Approach: Apply MH-DIF with ETS classification to METABENCH
46	        (5,227 models × 12,508 MMLU items)
47	      - >-
48	        Finding 1: 31–38% items functionally unstable across generations
49	        (31.3% temporal cohort primary, within-subject 31-45% avg 38.1%)
50	        — genuine capability evolution, not statistical artifact (sanity
51	        check 0.18%). [Architecture-stratified TBD: plan_010 running]
52	      - >-
53	        Finding 2: Web-overlap contamination labels do not capture
54	        differential contamination (enrichment≈1.0); semi-synthetic
55	        injection confirms DIF detection power (ΔTPR=+0.508 at p=0.5).
56	        Validation methodology gap affects entire field.
57	      - >-
58	        Finding 3: Semi-synthetic validation framework with cross-subject
59	        matching (ΔFPR=0.000) as reusable infrastructure; GSM8K replication
60	        confirms cross-benchmark portability (ΔTPR=+0.818)
61	      - >-
62	        Finding 4: DIF-flagged items concentrate cross-generational
63	        discriminative information — removing them disrupts rankings MORE
64	        than random removal (z=-8 to -49σ), while overall rankings stay
65	        robust (ρ>0.996). Cross-benchmark validation: DIF flags
66	        anti-correlate with GSM1K contamination gap (r=−0.478, 95%
67	        CI=[−0.71, −0.16], p=0.005) — DIF-C items resist contamination-
68	        based performance gains (suggestive, N=33).
69	        DIF is diagnostic lens, not item filter.
70	    dependencies: [experiments, method, discussion]
71	    registry_refs:
72	      - plan_001_real_data_dif_mmlu
73	      - plan_011_semi_synthetic_validation
74	      - plan_014_within_subject_dif
75	      - plan_016_within_subject_semi_synthetic
76	      - plan_017_downstream_impact
77	      - plan_004_gsm8k_cross_benchmark
78	
79	  - section: introduction
80	    word_budget: 1200
81	    core_bullets:
82	      - >-
83	        Hook: MMLU scores are treated as directly comparable across time —
84	        but 31% of items behave differently for 2024 vs 2023 model
85	        cohorts (ETS C DIF), persisting within every subject domain
86	        (31-45%, avg 38.1%)
87	      - >-
88	        Gap: Contamination detection research validates against web-overlap
89	        labels, but these measure global exposure, not differential item
90	        functioning — a fundamental validation methodology gap. All work
91	        using web-overlap/n-gram labels as ground truth for item-level
92	        detectors (including Min-K%, n-gram methods) has the same blind
93	        spot.
94	      - >-
95	        Insight: Applying classical psychometric DIF to LLM benchmarks
96	        reveals that item-level behavioral differences are pervasive and
97	        structural — three correction attempts (matched-ability,
98	        θ-conditioning, bifactor pre-check) all fail, pointing to genuine
99	        capability evolution as the dominant source
100	      - >-
101	        Tension resolution (Dream #3, MUST address in §1 end): "31%
102	        items unstable" sounds alarming but "ρ=0.997 ranking correlation"
103	        sounds reassuring. Resolve upfront: instability is real but
104	        concentrated in redundant measurement → benchmark robust at
105	        ranking level, fragile at item level. This is precisely why DIF
106	        is a diagnostic lens (understand what changed) not a quality
107	        filter (remove bad items).
108	      - >-
109	        Discovery process (anti-post-hoc framing): "We initially
110	        hypothesized DIF could detect contaminated items. Three structural
111	        improvements failed to separate contamination from capability
112	        evolution. This led us to investigate what persistent DIF actually
113	        captures." Pivot was data-driven: plan_011 semi-synthetic success
114	        (ΔTPR=+0.508) proved DIF works but ground truth labels don't —
115	        triggering problem redefinition. New evidence (plan_017 z=-49σ,
116	        plan_004 r=−0.478) came from post-pivot experiments, not
117	        reinterpretation of old data.
118	      - >-
119	        Novelty statement (MUST be explicit per Dream #3): We do not
120	        modify MH-DIF itself. Our novelty: (a) unprecedented scale
121	        (5,227 models) creates statistical challenges absent in
122	        educational testing; (b) cross-subject matching innovation
123	        eliminates FPR inflation; (c) ground truth meta-critique
124	        exposing validation methodology gap; (d) largest empirical
125	        characterization of item-level benchmark behavior.
126	      - >-
127	        Contributions: (C1) Benchmark temporal comparability concern —
128	        31% functional instability as empirical finding; (C2) Ground
129	        truth meta-critique — validation methodology gap in contamination
130	        detection literature; (C3) Semi-synthetic validation framework
131	        with cross-subject matching; (C4) DIF items concentrate
132	        discriminative information — diagnostic lens, not item filter
133	    dependencies: [experiments]

184	        3.1 Data: METABENCH response matrix (5,227 × 12,508) + Li et al.
185	        web-overlap labels (73.8% coverage, 9,229 items)
186	      - >-
187	        3.2 MH-DIF + ETS A/B/C classification — translate for ML audience:
188	        examinees→models, test items→benchmark questions, DIF→item-level
189	        behavioral anomaly conditional on ability. ETS thresholds: A
190	        (|Δ|<1.0), B (1.0≤|Δ|<1.5), C (|Δ|≥1.5)
191	      - >-
192	        3.3 Cohort designs: temporal (2023 vs 2024, N=1253/656),
193	        ability-quintile (Q1-2 vs Q4-5), within-family (Llama-2 N=161 vs
194	        Llama-3 N=308), within-subject (per-MMLU-subject DIF)
195	      - >-
196	        3.4 Semi-synthetic injection framework: select baseline-clean
197	        items (ETS A in uninjected data), inject contamination by flipping
198	        focal-group incorrect→correct responses at rate p ∈ {0.3,0.5,0.7,1.0},
199	        measure ΔTPR = TPR(injected) - TPR(baseline). Cross-subject
200	        matching: use total score on OTHER subjects as matching variable,
201	        avoiding matching variable contamination.
202	      - >-
203	        3.5 Diagnostics: Yen's Q3 for local independence, domain-specificity
204	        analysis (Spearman ρ between C% and accuracy improvement by subject)
205	      - >-
206	        3.6 Multiple testing considerations (Dream #3 required): ETS
207	        classification provides implicit protection via dual threshold
208	        (effect size |Δ_MH|≥1.5 AND significance p<0.05). BH FDR q=0.05
209	        correction removes only 3/3918 items (31.32%→31.30%) — ETS dual
210	        threshold already controls FPR. Random-split sanity check
211	        (C%=0.18%). Threshold sensitivity: C%=48.9% at 1.0, 31.3% at
212	        1.5 (standard), 18.3% at 2.0, 10.2% at 2.5. "Finding robust
213	        at standard thresholds; even at conservative 2.5, 1,278 items
214	        still exhibit large DIF." (plan_018). Architecture
215	        heterogeneity: non-issue (plan_010, 99.98% decoder-only).

334	      - >-
335	        5.1 Implications for benchmark temporal comparability: 31%
336	        instability (robust across thresholds: 10-49% at ETS 2.5-1.0)
337	        means cross-temporal MMLU scores carry uncontrolled item-level
338	        variance; instability decomposition shows 92.4% unrelated to
339	        domain accuracy improvement; benchmark designers should monitor
340	        DIF as quality diagnostic
341	      - >-
342	        5.2 Ground truth meta-critique — AGGRESSIVE framing per Director:
343	        all work validating item-level detectors against web-overlap/n-gram
344	        labels has the same validation methodology gap. Web-overlap measures
345	        existence, not differential usage. This is a meta-contribution to
346	        the contamination detection field — not just "DIF and Li et al.
347	        measure different things" but "the field's standard validation
348	        approach is fundamentally mismatched for item-level detection."
349	      - >-
350	        5.3a DIF as capability diagnostic (Claim 4 layer 4 discussion):
351	        GSM1K negative correlation reveals contamination produces "shallow"
352	        performance boost concentrated on non-DIF items, while DIF-C items
353	        capture genuine capability differences between model generations.
354	        171/249 focal-favoring DIF-C items (α<1) drive the effect — these
355	        are items where 2024 models genuinely improved, and contaminated
356	        models struggle disproportionately on them. MUST caveat: r=−0.478
357	        with CI=[−0.71, −0.16] is suggestive; item difficulty confound
358	        (DIF-C items may simply be harder) not fully excluded; N=33 limits
359	        generalizability. This is a paper highlight per Director but
360	        requires honest strength calibration.
361	      - >-
362	        5.3b Empirical observation on DIF applicability: 1D IRT fit
363	        limitations + power requirements + ability confounding jointly
364	        constrain DIF utility in LLM benchmarks. This is a structural
365	        constraint revealed by systematic experimentation, NOT a formal
366	        impossibility — higher-level methods (MIMIC, propensity-score
367	        matching, multidimensional IRT) may address individual constraints.
368	      - >-
369	        5.4 Limitations — MUST BE HONEST, non-negotiable:
370	        (a) ρ=0.307 ecological correlation between C% and accuracy
371	        improvement, but item-level decomposition (plan_019) shows
372	        domain improvement explains only 2.4pp (7.6%) of 31.3% C%.
373	        Still, cannot fully decompose remaining 92.4% into
374	        contamination vs other sources of capability change;
375	        (b) 38% C% cannot be decomposed into contamination vs capability;
376	        (c) semi-synthetic injection (incorrect→correct flipping) may
377	        not match real contamination patterns (partial knowledge, format
378	        memorization);
379	        (d) primarily MMLU/METABENCH — GSM8K cross-validation (§4.8)

383	        (e) cross-subject baseline FPR 33-53% — stable across injection

file.content:
meta:
  venue: ICLR 2027
  track: main
  template: ""
  template_note: "ICLR 2027 template not yet available locally; will download or reuse iclr2025 when entering Step 2"
  page_limit: 9
  deadline: "2026-10-01"
  core_claim: >-
    Applying DIF to MMLU (5,227 models × 12,508 items) reveals 38% item-level
    functional instability across model generations, exposes a fundamental gap
    in contamination ground truth labels, and provides a semi-synthetic
    validation framework for item-level detectors.
  created_at: "2026-05-20T23:45:00Z"
  story_arc:
    hook: >-
      When we say "Model B outperforms Model A on MMLU," we assume temporal
      comparability — but 38% of MMLU items function differently across model
      generations.
    gap: >-
      Existing contamination labels (web-overlap, n-gram) measure global
      exposure, not differential item functioning — every validation study
      using these labels has a blind spot. This is a fundamental validation
      methodology gap affecting the entire contamination detection field.
    insight: >-
      DIF detects differential contamination (semi-synthetic ΔTPR=+0.508) but
      temporal DIF is dominated by genuine capability evolution
      (enrichment≈1.0, within-subject C%=38.1%), and three structural
      corrections cannot separate them.
    mechanism: >-
      Semi-synthetic injection into real response matrices provides controlled
      ground truth; cross-subject matching eliminates FPR inflation (ΔFPR=0.000).
    evidence: >-
      38% items functionally unstable (plan_001/014); ΔTPR=+0.508 at p=0.5
      (plan_011); ΔFPR=0.000 cross-subject (plan_016); three improvements
      exhausted (plan_001b/012/014).

paper_outline:
  - section: abstract
    word_budget: 200
    core_bullets:
      - >-
        Problem: LLM benchmark scores assume temporal comparability, but
        item-level behavior may drift across model generations
      - >-
        Approach: Apply MH-DIF with ETS classification to METABENCH
        (5,227 models × 12,508 MMLU items)
      - >-
        Finding 1: 31–38% items functionally unstable across generations
        (31.3% temporal cohort primary, within-subject 31-45% avg 38.1%)
        — genuine capability evolution, not statistical artifact (sanity
        check 0.18%). [Architecture-stratified TBD: plan_010 running]
      - >-
        Finding 2: Web-overlap contamination labels do not capture
        differential contamination (enrichment≈1.0); semi-synthetic
        injection confirms DIF detection power (ΔTPR=+0.508 at p=0.5).
        Validation methodology gap affects entire field.
      - >-
        Finding 3: Semi-synthetic validation framework with cross-subject
        matching (ΔFPR=0.000) as reusable infrastructure; GSM8K replication
        confirms cross-benchmark portability (ΔTPR=+0.818)
      - >-
        Finding 4: DIF-flagged items concentrate cross-generational
        discriminative information — removing them disrupts rankings MORE
        than random removal (z=-8 to -49σ), while overall rankings stay
        robust (ρ>0.996). Cross-benchmark validation: DIF flags
        anti-correlate with GSM1K contamination gap (r=−0.478, 95%
        CI=[−0.71, −0.16], p=0.005) — DIF-C items resist contamination-
        based performance gains (suggestive, N=33).
        DIF is diagnostic lens, not item filter.
    dependencies: [experiments, method, discussion]
    registry_refs:
      - plan_001_real_data_dif_mmlu
      - plan_011_semi_synthetic_validation
      - plan_014_within_subject_dif
      - plan_016_within_subject_semi_synthetic
      - plan_017_downstream_impact
      - plan_004_gsm8k_cross_benchmark

  - section: introduction
    word_budget: 1200
    core_bullets:
      - >-
        Hook: MMLU scores are treated as directly comparable across time —
        but 31% of items behave differently for 2024 vs 2023 model
        cohorts (ETS C DIF), persisting within every subject domain
        (31-45%, avg 38.1%)
      - >-
        Gap: Contamination detection research validates against web-overlap
        labels, but these measure global exposure, not differential item
        functioning — a fundamental validation methodology gap. All work
        using web-overlap/n-gram labels as ground truth for item-level
        detectors (including Min-K%, n-gram methods) has the same blind
        spot.
      - >-
        Insight: Applying classical psychometric DIF to LLM benchmarks
        reveals that item-level behavioral differences are pervasive and
        structural — three correction attempts (matched-ability,
        θ-conditioning, bifactor pre-check) all fail, pointing to genuine
        capability evolution as the dominant source
      - >-
        Tension resolution (Dream #3, MUST address in §1 end): "31%
        items unstable" sounds alarming but "ρ=0.997 ranking correlation"
        sounds reassuring. Resolve upfront: instability is real but
        concentrated in redundant measurement → benchmark robust at
        ranking level, fragile at item level. This is precisely why DIF
        is a diagnostic lens (understand what changed) not a quality
        filter (remove bad items).
      - >-
        Discovery process (anti-post-hoc framing): "We initially
        hypothesized DIF could detect contaminated items. Three structural
        improvements failed to separate contamination from capability
        evolution. This led us to investigate what persistent DIF actually
        captures." Pivot was data-driven: plan_011 semi-synthetic success
        (ΔTPR=+0.508) proved DIF works but ground truth labels don't —
        triggering problem redefinition. New evidence (plan_017 z=-49σ,
        plan_004 r=−0.478) came from post-pivot experiments, not
        reinterpretation of old data.
      - >-
        Novelty statement (MUST be explicit per Dream #3): We do not
        modify MH-DIF itself. Our novelty: (a) unprecedented scale
        (5,227 models) creates statistical challenges absent in
        educational testing; (b) cross-subject matching innovation
        eliminates FPR inflation; (c) ground truth meta-critique
        exposing validation methodology gap; (d) largest empirical
        characterization of item-level benchmark behavior.
      - >-
        Contributions: (C1) Benchmark temporal comparability concern —
        31% functional instability as empirical finding; (C2) Ground
        truth meta-critique — validation methodology gap in contamination
        detection literature; (C3) Semi-synthetic validation framework
        with cross-subject matching; (C4) DIF items concentrate
        discriminative information — diagnostic lens, not item filter
    dependencies: [experiments]
    figures: [fig_1_global_vs_differential]
    citation_hints:
      - "METABENCH dataset citation"
      - "Li et al. (EMNLP 2024) web-overlap labels"
      - "Wang et al. (ICLR 2026) RL fragility — motivates psychometric approach"
      - "Growing Pains (Habba et al., NOT Polo) — positioning: they do score comparability, we do temporal stability characterization"

  - section: related_work
    word_budget: 800
    core_bullets:
      - >-
        Cluster 1: Contamination detection methods (Min-K%, ConStat, DVD,
        Self-Critique, n-gram baselines) — all validate against global
        exposure labels, not differential contamination; our meta-critique
        applies to their validation methodology
      - >-
        Cluster 2: IRT in LLM evaluation (Growing Pains [Habba et al.],
        PSN-IRT [Zhou et al.], Hardy scalability, Lalor 2019, Vania
        2021) — DEDICATED technical comparison with Growing Pains: they
        use anchor items for efficient extensible evaluation; our DIF
        diagnostic tells them WHICH anchor items are degrading across
        model generations. Mutual value: their framework + our
        diagnostic = monitored extensible evaluation. Complementary not
        competing. (R2-W2)
      - >-
        Cluster 3: DIF methodology — MH-DIF (Holland & Thayer 1988), ETS
        classification, non-uniform DIF (Swaminathan & Rogers 1990),
        IRT-based alternatives (Lord's χ², Raju's area), SIBTEST (Shealy
        & Stout 1993), logistic regression DIF (Clauser & Mazor 1998,
        Zumbo 1999), small-sample DIF (Belzak 2020), propensity score
        matching for DIF (Teresi 2007). Our application context is novel;
        method itself is established; we acknowledge impact-vs-DIF
        confound as central challenge.
      - >-
        Cluster 4: Measurement invariance (Meredith 1993, Vandenberg &
        Lance 2000) — DIF is item-level test of measurement invariance;
        our work is the first large-scale measurement invariance analysis
        of LLM benchmarks. Frame DIF within broader invariance testing
        tradition.
      - >-
        Cluster 5: Benchmark design and concurrent work (LiveBench,
        GAIA, Chatbot Arena, dynamic benchmarks) — we characterize
        existing benchmarks psychometrically, they build new ones or
        use alternative evaluation paradigms
    dependencies: [introduction]

  - section: method
    word_budget: 1400
    core_bullets:
      - >-
        3.1 Data: METABENCH response matrix (5,227 × 12,508) + Li et al.
        web-overlap labels (73.8% coverage, 9,229 items)
      - >-
        3.2 MH-DIF + ETS A/B/C classification — translate for ML audience:
        examinees→models, test items→benchmark questions, DIF→item-level
        behavioral anomaly conditional on ability. ETS thresholds: A
        (|Δ|<1.0), B (1.0≤|Δ|<1.5), C (|Δ|≥1.5)
      - >-
        3.3 Cohort designs: temporal (2023 vs 2024, N=1253/656),
        ability-quintile (Q1-2 vs Q4-5), within-family (Llama-2 N=161 vs
        Llama-3 N=308), within-subject (per-MMLU-subject DIF)
      - >-
        3.4 Semi-synthetic injection framework: select baseline-clean
        items (ETS A in uninjected data), inject contamination by flipping
        focal-group incorrect→correct responses at rate p ∈ {0.3,0.5,0.7,1.0},
        measure ΔTPR = TPR(injected) - TPR(baseline). Cross-subject
        matching: use total score on OTHER subjects as matching variable,
        avoiding matching variable contamination.
      - >-
        3.5 Diagnostics: Yen's Q3 for local independence, domain-specificity
        analysis (Spearman ρ between C% and accuracy improvement by subject)
      - >-
        3.6 Multiple testing considerations (Dream #3 required): ETS
        classification provides implicit protection via dual threshold
        (effect size |Δ_MH|≥1.5 AND significance p<0.05). BH FDR q=0.05
        correction removes only 3/3918 items (31.32%→31.30%) — ETS dual
        threshold already controls FPR. Random-split sanity check
        (C%=0.18%). Threshold sensitivity: C%=48.9% at 1.0, 31.3% at
        1.5 (standard), 18.3% at 2.0, 10.2% at 2.5. "Finding robust
        at standard thresholds; even at conservative 2.5, 1,278 items
        still exhibit large DIF." (plan_018). Architecture
        heterogeneity: non-issue (plan_010, 99.98% decoder-only).
    dependencies: []
    notation_table:
      θ: "latent ability (IRT)"
      Δ_MH: "Mantel-Haenszel DIF statistic (log-odds ratio)"
      p: "exploitation rate in semi-synthetic injection"
      "C%": "percentage of items classified ETS C (large DIF)"
      ΔTPR: "TPR increase from injection over baseline"
      ΔFPR: "FPR change from injection (should be 0 for valid framework)"

  - section: experiments
    word_budget: 2500
    core_bullets:
      - >-
        4.1 Validation: DIF works under controlled conditions — power
        analysis with real MMLU IRT parameters, ETS C TPR=0.68-0.80 at
        N≥80 δ≥1.4, FPR=0.036-0.042, AUC 0.93-0.94
      - >-
        4.2 Temporal comparability concern: 31.3% ETS C (temporal,
        primary estimate; BH-corrected 31.30%), sanity random split
        0.18%, within-family Llama-2v3 61.3% (ability confound),
        ability-quintile 2.9% (well-controlled), domain ρ=0.307
        (p=0.02). Within-subject C%=38.1% (31-45% across 5 subjects)
        — instability penetrates within every domain. Instability
        decomposition (plan_019): ρ=0.307 is ecological correlation;
        item-level domain improvement explains only 2.4pp of 31.3%
        (pseudo R²=0.0007, counterfactual C%=29.0%). 92.4% of
        instability is unrelated to domain accuracy improvement.
        Use Model 1 (no causal assumptions) as primary; Model 2
        shows Simpson's paradox (supplementary).
        Architecture heterogeneity (plan_010): non-issue — METABENCH
        MMLU is 99.98% decoder-only (5226/5227), excluding the 1
        non-decoder model yields C%=31.32% (Jaccard=1.0 with full
        population). IRT person-fit (98% |Lz|>2) reflects MMLU's
        57-subject multidimensionality, not architecture heterogeneity.
      - >-
        4.3 Ground truth mismatch: enrichment=0.96 against Li et al.
        web-overlap labels; semi-synthetic ΔTPR=+0.508 (p=0.5), +0.674
        (p=1.0), clear dose-response; DIF WORKS for differential
        contamination but Li et al. labels are the wrong ground truth
      - >-
        4.4 Structural analysis — empirical observation that three
        structural improvements fail: (a) matched-ability enrichment
        0.94-1.04 (main text 1 sentence → Appendix A.x for detail),
        (b) θ-conditioning r=0.9986 FPR unchanged at 31% (Appendix A.y
        "Structural Constraints"), (c) within-subject pre-check C%=38.1%
        (bifactor not viable). Frame as: jointly constraining DIF utility,
        not formal impossibility. [Reviewer allocation: plan_001b main=1
        sentence, plan_012 appendix-only]
      - >-
        4.5 Semi-synthetic framework validation: cross-subject matching
        ΔFPR=0.000 all 5 subjects, 4/5 ΔTPR>0.3 at p=0.5 (cross), vs
        within-subject FPR inflation +0.186. Cross-subject matching as
        methodological recommendation.
      - >-
        4.6 Q3 local independence: 11.3% within-subject pairs >0.20 vs
        2.2% cross-subject (5x, p=2.3e-9); mild local dependence,
        contributing factor but not main FPR driver
      - >-
        4.7 Downstream impact — four layers: (1) Benchmark redundancy:
        ρ≈0.997 full vs stable-only, rankings extremely robust to 31%
        removal; (2) DIF items carry more signal than average items
        (z=-8 to -49σ vs random, 21/21), BUT circularity ablation
        (plan_020) shows DIF is the LEAST disruptive non-random strategy:
        high-discrimination z=-15.8, accuracy-gap z=-156.5, high-variance
        z=-107.9 vs DIF z=-9.5. DIF specifically isolates ability-
        conditioned differential behavior, not just generally informative
        items. DIF-discrimination Jaccard=0.12 (orthogonal constructs).
        DO NOT simultaneously claim "signal carriers" and "conservative
        filter" — use: "DIF items carry more signal than average but
        DIF isolates differential behavior specifically."
        (3) DIF as diagnostic lens: identifies which capability
        dimensions drive ranking shifts across generations. Model-specific
        patterns (phi-3/llama-3 +700-850, mistral merges -400 to -587)
        but caveat: top-50 movers 49/50 "unknown" family;
        (4) Cross-benchmark validation: GSM1K contamination gap
        anti-correlates with DIF advantage (r=−0.478, 95% CI=[−0.71,
        −0.16], p=0.005) — DIF-C items resist contamination-based
        performance gains (N=33, partial r=−0.385 controlling accuracy,
        permutation p=0.014). Suggestive not conclusive; item difficulty
        confound cannot be fully excluded at N=33.
      - >-
        4.8 Cross-benchmark validation (GSM8K, 1,319 items × 6,702 models):
        Three-part analysis. (a) Temporal DIF: C%=18.9% (standard matching),
        sanity 0.3% — instability is lower than MMLU (31.3%) but still
        substantial for a single-domain benchmark. (b) Semi-synthetic:
        ΔTPR=+0.818 (standard, p=0.7), +0.517 (external, p=0.7); dose-
        response confirmed; framework generalizes beyond MMLU.
        (c) GSM1K contamination gap correlation: DIF-C items anti-correlate
        with contamination gap (r=−0.478, 95% CI=[−0.71, −0.16], p=0.005;
        partial r=−0.385 controlling accuracy; permutation p=0.014, N=33).
        MUST honestly report: original hypothesis predicted POSITIVE
        correlation (contaminated models gain on DIF items); observed
        NEGATIVE direction — DIF-C items resist contamination-based gains.
        Suggestive at N=33; item difficulty confound not fully excluded.
        [Reviewer: 1 paragraph + fig_5, honest hypothesis vs result]
    dependencies: []
    registry_refs:
      - mvp_dif_power_sim
      - mvp_dif_power_sim_phase2
      - plan_001_real_data_dif_mmlu
      - plan_001b_matched_ability_dif
      - plan_011_semi_synthetic_validation
      - plan_012_irt_theta_conditioning
      - plan_013_q3_local_independence
      - plan_014_within_subject_dif
      - plan_016_within_subject_semi_synthetic
      - plan_017_downstream_impact
      - plan_018_ets_threshold_sensitivity
      - plan_019_instability_decomposition
      - plan_010_architecture_stratified_dif
      - plan_020_circularity_ablation
      - plan_004_gsm8k_cross_benchmark
    tables: [tab_1_temporal_landscape, tab_2_structural_comparison]
    figures: [fig_2_dose_response, fig_3_within_subject_matching, fig_4_downstream_impact, fig_5_gsm1k_dif_correlation]

  - section: discussion
    word_budget: 1000
    core_bullets:
      - >-
        5.1 Implications for benchmark temporal comparability: 31%
        instability (robust across thresholds: 10-49% at ETS 2.5-1.0)
        means cross-temporal MMLU scores carry uncontrolled item-level
        variance; instability decomposition shows 92.4% unrelated to
        domain accuracy improvement; benchmark designers should monitor
        DIF as quality diagnostic
      - >-
        5.2 Ground truth meta-critique — AGGRESSIVE framing per Director:
        all work validating item-level detectors against web-overlap/n-gram
        labels has the same validation methodology gap. Web-overlap measures
        existence, not differential usage. This is a meta-contribution to
        the contamination detection field — not just "DIF and Li et al.
        measure different things" but "the field's standard validation
        approach is fundamentally mismatched for item-level detection."
      - >-
        5.3a DIF as capability diagnostic (Claim 4 layer 4 discussion):
        GSM1K negative correlation reveals contamination produces "shallow"
        performance boost concentrated on non-DIF items, while DIF-C items
        capture genuine capability differences between model generations.
        171/249 focal-favoring DIF-C items (α<1) drive the effect — these
        are items where 2024 models genuinely improved, and contaminated
        models struggle disproportionately on them. MUST caveat: r=−0.478
        with CI=[−0.71, −0.16] is suggestive; item difficulty confound
        (DIF-C items may simply be harder) not fully excluded; N=33 limits
        generalizability. This is a paper highlight per Director but
        requires honest strength calibration.
      - >-
        5.3b Empirical observation on DIF applicability: 1D IRT fit
        limitations + power requirements + ability confounding jointly
        constrain DIF utility in LLM benchmarks. This is a structural
        constraint revealed by systematic experimentation, NOT a formal
        impossibility — higher-level methods (MIMIC, propensity-score
        matching, multidimensional IRT) may address individual constraints.
      - >-
        5.4 Limitations — MUST BE HONEST, non-negotiable:
        (a) ρ=0.307 ecological correlation between C% and accuracy
        improvement, but item-level decomposition (plan_019) shows
        domain improvement explains only 2.4pp (7.6%) of 31.3% C%.
        Still, cannot fully decompose remaining 92.4% into
        contamination vs other sources of capability change;
        (b) 38% C% cannot be decomposed into contamination vs capability;
        (c) semi-synthetic injection (incorrect→correct flipping) may
        not match real contamination patterns (partial knowledge, format
        memorization);
        (d) primarily MMLU/METABENCH — GSM8K cross-validation (§4.8)
        confirms semi-synthetic framework portability and provides GSM1K
        correlation evidence (N=33), but full temporal DIF characterization
        on diverse benchmarks not yet done; GSM1K N=33 has wide CI;
        (e) cross-subject baseline FPR 33-53% — stable across injection
        levels but not low;
        (f) RL robustness: theoretically motivated but empirically
        unvalidated with adequate sample size (N=13 reasoning-RL models
        in METABENCH);
        (g) downstream impact family analysis limited to N≥20 families
        (llama, mistral, qwen, phi); top-50 rank movers 49/50 are
        "unknown" family — family-level conclusions have limited coverage
      - >-
        5.5 Future work (SCOPE REDUCED per Dream #3 — main text only
        lists directions, no extended discussion): broader cross-
        benchmark generalization, RL model cohorts with adequate N,
        MIMIC models for confound control. [Appendix-only: Bayesian DIF,
        ensemble fusion (DIF + ConStat + DVD), complementary baselines,
        pilot studies (bifactor equating, item generation), SIBTEST/LR-DIF
        comparison, item-focused trees]
    dependencies: [experiments]

  - section: conclusion
    word_budget: 350
    core_bullets:
      - >-
        Four contributions: (1) 38% MMLU items functionally unstable
        across model generations, (2) ground truth meta-critique —
        validation methodology gap in contamination detection, (3)
        semi-synthetic framework with cross-subject matching (cross-
        benchmark replication on GSM8K: ΔTPR=+0.818), (4) DIF as
        diagnostic lens — four-layer finding
      - >-
        Key message: LLM benchmarks need psychometric monitoring, not
        just score reporting — DIF reveals benchmark quality as a
        benchmark quality tool
      - >-
        DIF items concentrate discriminative information (removal disrupts
        rankings MORE than random, z=-8 to -49σ) and anti-correlate with
        contamination gap (r=−0.478, CI=[−0.71, −0.16]) — DIF-C items
        resist contamination-based performance gains (suggestive, N=33)
    dependencies: [experiments, discussion]

visualization_plan:
  - fig_id: fig_1_global_vs_differential
    type: conceptual
    tool: paperbanana
    description: >-
      Global vs Differential contamination concept diagram with ICC
      illustration — global exposure affects all models equally (no DIF),
      differential training data inclusion creates group-specific ICC
      shifts (DIF detected). Shows why enrichment≈1.0 is expected.
    narrative_intent: >-
      Web-overlap labels and DIF measure fundamentally different things:
      global exposure vs differential item functioning. Low enrichment is
      expected, not failure.
    design_notes:
      - >-
        Left panel: "Global Contamination" — item on Common Crawl since
        2020, both cohort ICCs overlap (no DIF), Li et al. labels it
        contaminated but DIF correctly reports no group difference
      - >-
        Right panel: "Differential Contamination" — item in focal
        cohort's training data only, ICCs diverge (DIF detected), Li
        et al. may or may not label it
      - >-
        Use ICC curves (S-shaped logistic) with shaded area between
        curves = DIF magnitude (Δ_MH)
      - "Color: reference cohort blue, focal cohort orange (Okabe-Ito)"
      - >-
        Bottom annotation connecting panels: "Enrichment ≈ 1.0 because
        most MMLU items are globally contaminated (left), not
        differentially (right)"
    placement: introduction
    aspect_ratio: "16:9"

  - fig_id: fig_2_dose_response
    type: statistical
    tool: matplotlib
    description: >-
      Semi-synthetic dose-response: TPR vs exploitation rate p for
      temporal cohort with external/cross-subject matching, plus FPR
      stability panel
    narrative_intent: >-
      DIF detection power increases monotonically with contamination
      exploitation rate (clear dose-response), and cross-subject matching
      maintains perfectly stable FPR (ΔFPR=0.000) — controlled detection
      capability confirmed.
    design_notes:
      - "x-axis: exploitation rate p ∈ {0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0}"
      - >-
        Top panel: TPR lines — temporal_external (primary, solid blue),
        temporal_standard (dashed red, shows FPR inflation problem at
        high p)
      - >-
        Bottom panel (smaller): FPR vs p — external flat at ~0.31
        (ΔFPR=0.000), standard inflating from 0.30 to 0.62
      - "Pattern A: light regime band at p<0.3 labeled 'below practical detection'"
      - "Dashed horizontal lines at baseline TPR (p=0) for reference"
      - "Annotate ΔTPR=+0.508 at p=0.5 on the primary line"
    data_source: "registry: plan_011_semi_synthetic_validation"
    placement: experiments
    aspect_ratio: "3:4"

  - fig_id: fig_3_within_subject_matching
    type: statistical
    tool: matplotlib
    description: >-
      Within-subject semi-synthetic: 5 subjects comparing cross-subject
      vs within-subject matching on ΔTPR and ΔFPR
    narrative_intent: >-
      Cross-subject matching eliminates FPR inflation (ΔFPR=0.000 for
      all 5 subjects) while maintaining detection power — a practical
      methodological recommendation.
    design_notes:
      - >-
        Paired dot plot or grouped bars: 5 subjects on x-axis, sorted
        by cross-subject ΔTPR
      - >-
        Left panel: ΔTPR at p=0.5 — cross (filled circle) vs within
        (open circle), connected by line
      - >-
        Right panel: ΔFPR — cross all at 0.000 (flat line), within
        showing inflation (+0.067 to +0.281)
      - "Reference line: ΔTPR=0.3 (success threshold), ΔFPR=0"
      - >-
        Highlight business_ethics: high baseline FPR (0.53-0.56),
        negative within-subject ΔTPR, low cross-subject ΔTPR — the
        failure case
    data_source: "registry: plan_016_within_subject_semi_synthetic"
    placement: experiments
    aspect_ratio: "3:2"

  - fig_id: fig_4_downstream_impact
    type: statistical
    tool: matplotlib
    description: >-
      Model-level rank change scatter: full-benchmark rank vs
      stable-only rank, showing that DIF removal systematically
      disrupts rankings more than random removal. Annotate key model
      clusters (phi-3/llama-3 beneficiaries, mistral merge losers).
    narrative_intent: >-
      DIF-flagged items concentrate cross-generational discriminative
      information — removing them disrupts rankings MORE than random
      removal, revealing model-specific evolution patterns rather than
      benchmark noise.
    design_notes:
      - >-
        Scatter plot: x = full-benchmark rank, y = stable-only rank.
        Diagonal line (y=x) = no change. Points above = gained rank
        (benefited from DIF items), below = lost rank.
      - >-
        Color by model family or cohort (2023 blue, 2024 orange) if
        feasible; otherwise uniform gray with key models highlighted
      - >-
        Annotate clusters: phi-3 / llama-3 derivatives (large positive
        rank change, +700-850), mistral merges (large negative, -400
        to -587)
      - >-
        Inset or annotation box: ρ_full_vs_stable = 0.996, z_dif_vs_random
        = -14.9 (mean), DIF items 1.09× cross-cohort ratio
      - "Reference diagonal dashed line y=x"
      - "Alternative: if scatter too dense, use hexbin or contour"
    data_source: "registry: plan_017_downstream_impact"
    placement: experiments
    aspect_ratio: "4:3"

  - fig_id: fig_5_gsm1k_dif_correlation
    type: statistical
    tool: matplotlib
    description: >-
      GSM1K contamination gap vs DIF advantage scatter: 33 matched models,
      showing significant negative correlation (r=−0.478, p=0.005).
      Models with higher contamination (GSM8K−GSM1K gap) perform WORSE
      on DIF-C items — DIF captures capability, not contamination.
    narrative_intent: >-
      Cross-benchmark validation of Claim 4's "DIF as diagnostic lens":
      contaminated models cannot fake performance on DIF items, which
      capture genuine capability-discriminative differences. The negative
      correlation inverts the contamination narrative.
    design_notes:
      - >-
        Scatter: x = GSM8K−GSM1K contamination gap, y = DIF advantage
        (acc_DIF_C − acc_non_DIF). Regression line with 95% CI band.
      - >-
        Color by model family (Phi green, Gemma orange, Llama blue,
        Mixtral purple, DeepSeek red, Other gray)
      - "Annotate: r=−0.478, p=0.005 (partial r=−0.385 ctrl accuracy)"
      - "Annotate key outlier: Deepseek-math-7b-rl (near zero on both)"
      - >-
        Dashed horizontal line at DIF advantage = 0; most models below
        (DIF items are harder for all, but contaminated models worse)
      - "Already generated by Agent Worker — may need style refinement"
    data_source: "registry: plan_004_gsm8k_cross_benchmark, artifacts/plan_004/gsm1k_dif_correlation.csv"

    aspect_ratio: "4:3"
    source_file: "artifacts/plan_004/fig_gsm1k_dif_correlation.pdf"

  - fig_id: fig_A1_subject_heatmap

      Item instability is pervasive across all MMLU subjects, not

table_plan:

    placement: experiments

      within-family (Llama-2 vs Llama-3), random split (sanity check),
      within-subject average (5 subjects). Highlight contrast: sanity
      0.18% vs temporal 31.3%. Within-subject 38.1% proves instability
      penetrates within domains.

  - table_id: tab_2_structural_comparison
    caption: >-

      reduces temporal baseline FPR below 31%.
    placement: experiments

    notes: >-
      Rows: baseline (plan_011 external matching), matched-ability
      quintiles (plan_001b), IRT θ-conditioning (plan_012), within-subject
      pre-check (plan_014). Frame as "empirical observation revealing
      structural constraint" not "our method failed." Note: higher-level
      methods (MIMIC, propensity-score) may address individual constraints.
    baseline_row: "Baseline (plan_011 external matching, FPR=0.314, TPR=0.834)"

  - table_id: tab_3_gsm8k_comparison
    caption: >-
      Cross-benchmark comparison: MMLU vs GSM8K on temporal DIF and
      semi-synthetic detection. GSM8K replicates key findings on a
      single-domain math benchmark (1,319 items × 6,702 models).
    placement: experiments
    type: comparison
    columns:
      - Metric
      - MMLU (plan_001/011)
      - GSM8K (plan_004)
    data_source: "registry: plan_001_real_data_dif_mmlu, plan_011_semi_synthetic_validation, plan_004_gsm8k_cross_benchmark"

      (external) / GSM1K gap correlation (GSM8K only). Highlight: GSM8K

  - table_id: tab_A1_power_analysis
    caption: >-
      DIF power analysis: ETS C classification performance with real

    placement: appendix
    type: statistics
    columns:

      - "δ (logits)"
      - TPR (ETS C)
      - FPR (ETS C)

  - table_id: tab_A3_threshold_sensitivity
    caption: >-
      ETS threshold sensitivity analysis with BH FDR correction (q=0.05).
      Finding robust across thresholds; BH correction removes only 3
      items at standard threshold.
    placement: appendix
    type: statistics
    columns:
      - "ETS Threshold (|Δ_MH|)"
      - "C% (uncorrected)"
      - "C% (BH-corrected)"
      - "N items flagged"
    data_source: "registry: plan_018_ets_threshold_sensitivity"
    notes: >-
      Rows: 1.0 (48.9%/48.2%), 1.5 (31.3%/31.3%), 2.0 (18.3%/18.3%),
      2.5 (10.2%/10.2%). BH has minimal effect because ETS dual
      threshold (effect size + significance) already controls FPR.

  - table_id: tab_A4_circularity_ablation
    caption: >-
      Circularity ablation: ranking disruption from removing different
      item subsets (31.3% removal rate). DIF is least disruptive
      non-random strategy.
    placement: appendix
    type: comparison
    columns:
      - Removal Strategy
      - "ρ (2024 cohort)"
      - "z vs random"
      - "Jaccard with DIF-C"
    data_source: "registry: plan_020_circularity_ablation"
    notes: >-
      DIF z=-9.5 vs random, but high-discrimination z=-15.8,
      accuracy-gap z=-156.5, high-variance z=-107.9. DIF-discrimination
      Jaccard=0.12. DIF isolates ability-conditioned differential
      behavior, not just generally informative items.

DIF enrichment≈1.0 against Li et al. labels is expected, not failure — these labels cannot evaluate item-level differential detectors. This is a fundamental validation methodology gap: all work using web-overlap labels as ground truth for item-level detectors (including Min-K%, n-gram methods) has the same blind spot. Semi-synthetic injection confirms DIF can detect differential contamination (ΔTPR=+0.508 at p=0.5, dose-response from p=0.3 to p=1.0).
- Evidence: plan_001 (enrichment=0.96), plan_011 (ΔTPR=+0.508, dose-response)
- Framing: aggressive — "the field's standard validation approach is fundamentally mismatched for item-level detection"

**Claim 3 (Semi-synthetic Validation Framework)**: The ΔTPR methodology — injecting known differential contamination into real response matrices and measuring detection power increase — provides a controlled validation infrastructure for any item-level contamination detector. Cross-subject matching (using total score on OTHER subjects as MH matching variable) eliminates FPR inflation (ΔFPR=0.000 across all 5 tested subjects), while within-subject matching suffers from matching variable contamination (FPR inflation +0.186).
- Evidence: plan_011, plan_016 (ΔFPR=0.000 cross-subject, 4/5 subjects ΔTPR>0.3), plan_004 Step 2 (GSM8K ΔTPR=+0.818 standard, +0.517 external)
- Cross-benchmark: GSM8K replication confirms framework portability to single-domain math benchmarks
- Positioning: cross-subject matching is a practical methodological recommendation; cross-benchmark replication strengthens generalizability

**Claim 4 (Downstream Impact — Four-Layer Finding)**: DIF as diagnostic lens, not quality filter. Four sub-findings:
1. **Benchmark redundancy**: ρ≈0.997 between full and stable-only rankings — MMLU rankings are extremely robust to 31% item removal, revealing massive measurement redundancy in the benchmark.
2. **DIF items carry cross-cohort signal but are NOT the most ranking-defining items**: DIF removal causes MORE disruption than random removal (z=-8 to -49σ, 21/21 conditions), confirming DIF items are non-trivial. But circularity ablation (plan_020) shows DIF is the LEAST disruptive non-random strategy: accuracy-gap removal disrupts 10-16× more (z=-157 vs -9.5), high-variance 11× more (z=-108), high-discrimination 1.7× more (z=-16). MH's ability conditioning filters out raw accuracy differences, isolating genuine differential functioning rather than generally informative items. DIF-discrimination overlap is only 22.1% (Jaccard=0.12) — DIF identifies "items that changed across generations," not "good items."
3. **DIF as diagnostic lens**: DIF identifies which items' functioning changes most across model generations → reveals which capability dimensions drive ranking shifts. Not "find bad items and remove" but "understand what changed and why." Model-specific patterns: phi-3/llama-3 gain +700-850 ranks from DIF items, mistral merges lose -400 to -587.
4. **Cross-benchmark validation — DIF items resist contamination-based gains**: On GSM8K (1,319 items × 6,702 models), DIF flags anti-correlate with GSM1K contamination gap (r=−0.478, p=0.005, 95% BCa CI [−0.714, −0.155]; Spearman ρ=−0.403, p=0.020, CI [−0.687, −0.031]; partial r=−0.385 controlling GSM8K accuracy, p=0.030, CI [−0.640, −0.058]; permutation p=0.014). All CIs exclude zero. Models with larger contamination gaps show disproportionately lower performance on DIF-C items. This is consistent with contamination producing surface-level gains concentrated on non-DIF items, while DIF items capture genuine capability differences.
- Evidence: plan_017 (z=-8 to -49σ, ρ=0.996-0.999), plan_020 (circularity ablation: DIF z=-9.5 vs acc-gap z=-157, disc z=-16, var z=-108), plan_004 Step 3 (r=−0.478, p=0.005, N=33)
- Architecture: plan_017 is load-bearing (strong, full N=5,227), Step 3 adds contamination dimension but is suggestive (N=33, CI wide). If Step 3 attacked, plan_017 stands independently.
- Growing Pains互补: "Growing Pains uses anchor items for efficient evaluation; our DIF diagnostic tells them which anchor items are degrading"
- Caveats (→ limitations): N=33, Pearson CI upper bound |r|=0.155 (small effect possible), Spearman CI upper bound |ρ|=0.031 (near zero possible); item difficulty confound not fully excluded (DIF-C items harder for all models); contamination gap is proxy, not ground truth; replication with larger matched sample needed

## Story Spine (v2 — no-pivot narrative)

**Opening frame**: LLM benchmarks implicitly assume temporal score comparability — when we say "Model B outperforms Model A on MMLU," we presume both scores reflect the same latent construct. But do they? Psychometrics has a mature tool for testing exactly this: Differential Item Functioning (DIF) analysis detects items whose difficulty changes across examinee groups after controlling for overall ability. We apply MH-DIF to the METABENCH response matrix (5,227 models × 12,508 MMLU items) — the largest-scale DIF analysis on LLM benchmarks to date.

**Key narrative principle**: "Instability ≠ invalidity." DIF flags items whose functioning changed across generations — this is a diagnostic signal, not a quality verdict. MMLU rankings are massively redundant (ρ≈0.997 after removing 31% of items), so instability doesn't threaten validity. But it reveals WHICH capability dimensions are shifting. **This framing must appear in the Introduction, not be deferred to Discussion.**

**What we find** (4 contributions, focused):

1. **31% of MMLU items are functionally unstable** across model generations (ETS C, |Δ_MH|≥1.5). Robust to threshold choice (49%/31%/18%/10% at 1.0/1.5/2.0/2.5), multiple testing (BH removes 3/3918 items), and architecture composition (99.98% decoder-only). Domain accuracy improvement explains ≤2.4pp of 31.3% C% (7.6%; pseudo R²=0.0007). The instability is predominantly item-specific, not a proxy for "models got better."

2. **Ground truth meta-critique**: Web-overlap contamination labels measure global exposure, not differential contamination. Enrichment≈1.0 is expected. Semi-synthetic injection confirms DIF detects differential contamination (ΔTPR=+0.508). Any item-level detector validated against web-overlap labels has this blind spot.

3. **Semi-synthetic validation framework**: ΔTPR methodology with cross-subject matching (ΔFPR=0.000). Portable across benchmarks (GSM8K ΔTPR=+0.818). Reusable for validating any item-level contamination detector.

4. **DIF as diagnostic lens**: DIF items carry cross-cohort signal (z=-8 to -49σ vs random) but are the LEAST disruptive non-random strategy (z=-9.5 vs accuracy-gap z=-157). DIF isolates genuine differential functioning, not just informative items. Cross-benchmark: DIF items resist contamination-based gains (r=−0.478, BCa CI [−0.71, −0.16]).

**Headline result**: "Psychometric DIF analysis of 5,227 models × 12,508 MMLU items reveals 31% temporal instability — robust across thresholds, not driven by capability improvement (≤7.6%), and not a validity threat (ρ≈0.997 ranking stability). The field's web-overlap ground truth cannot capture this differential signal; we provide a semi-synthetic validation framework with cross-subject matching (ΔFPR=0.000). DIF items resist contamination-based gains (r=−0.478) and serve as a diagnostic lens for understanding what changed across model generations."

## Scope Control (main body vs appendix)

**MAIN BODY (4 claims + robustness)**:
- §1 Introduction (problem + "instability ≠ invalidity" framing upfront)
- §2 Related Work (45 papers, 5 clusters)
- §3 Method (MH-DIF primer, semi-synthetic framework, cross-subject matching)
- §4 Experiments: Claim 1 (temporal DIF + threshold + BH + decomposition + architecture), Claim 2 (enrichment + meta-critique), Claim 3 (semi-synthetic + cross-benchmark), Claim 4 (redundancy + circularity ablation + diagnostic lens + GSM1K validation)
- §5 Discussion + Limitations
- §6 Conclusion

**APPENDIX (pruned from main body)**:
- Bayesian cumulative DIF (plan_007) — simulation-only, underdeveloped
- RL robustness (plan_002) — N=13, underpowered
- Ensemble fusion (plan_003a/b/c) — negative, not executed
- Bifactor equating pilot — below target fit
- Item generation pilot — below benchmarks
- Graceful degradation — clean but supplementary
- Item-Focused Trees — robustness check, supplementary
- ConStat/DVD comparisons — complementary baselines

## Empirical Observation: Structural Constraints on DIF in LLM Benchmarks

Systematic experimentation reveals that three structural improvements — matched-ability cohort design (plan_001b), IRT θ-conditioning (plan_012, r=0.9986), and bifactor pre-check (plan_014, within-subject C%=38.1%) — all fail to reduce temporal DIF baseline FPR below 31% while maintaining detection power. This is an empirical observation, not a formal impossibility result. The constraints arise from: (a) unidimensional IRT limitations in modeling 57-subject multidimensional ability, (b) statistical power requirements (N≥80, δ≥1.4), and (c) inability to separate ability confounding from genuine item-level changes. Higher-level methods (MIMIC, propensity-score matching, multidimensional IRT) may address individual constraints — future work.

## Venue Fit

- **ICLR 2027**: Good fit — empirical analysis of evaluation methodology, psychometric rigor, large-scale characterization. Risk: ML reviewers may not be familiar with DIF/IRT. Mitigation: §3 provides self-contained DIF primer with ML translations.

## Novelty Articulation (三层，显式化)

MH-DIF (1959/1988) is applied without modification. **Explicitly acknowledge this.** Novelty is NOT algorithmic. Three layers of genuine contribution:

1. **Empirical discovery at unprecedented scale**: First DIF analysis on 5,227×12,508 LLM response matrix. Finding: 31% temporal instability is robust across thresholds (10-49%), not explained by capability improvement (≤7.6%), and architecturally homogeneous (99.98% decoder-only). No prior work has characterized item-level stability of LLM benchmarks at this scale. The instability finding itself is new data about MMLU's measurement properties.

2. **Ground truth meta-critique with field-wide implications**: The observation that web-overlap labels cannot validate item-level differential detectors is NOT obvious — the field routinely uses them. This affects the validity claims of Min-K%, ConStat, n-gram methods, and all papers using web-overlap as ground truth. First empirical demonstration (enrichment≈1.0 + semi-synthetic proof).

3. **Semi-synthetic validation framework + cross-subject matching**: The ΔTPR methodology is a reusable infrastructure contribution. Cross-subject matching (ΔFPR=0.000) is a novel practical innovation — the insight that within-subject matching contaminates the conditioning variable is subtle and general. Portable to any multi-domain benchmark (demonstrated on GSM8K).

**Framing**: "We bring mature psychometric tools to characterize an urgent ML evaluation problem. The contribution is the empirical findings, the validation methodology critique, and the reusable framework — not a new algorithm."

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns (updated for pivot)

1. **"38% could just mean models got better"** — ✅ RESOLVED (plan_019). Item-level decomposition shows domain improvement explains ≤2.4pp of 31.3% C% (7.6%). Subject-level ρ=0.307 is an ecological correlation that grossly overstates the item-level relationship (pseudo R²=0.0007). The instability is predominantly item-specific. Present Model 1 (2.4pp) as primary; acknowledge confounder-vs-mediator ambiguity in Model 2 as honest discussion.

2. **"Ground truth critique is obvious — of course web labels don't capture differential effects"** — Not obvious: the field routinely uses these labels for item-level validation. We provide the first empirical demonstration with both the enrichment≈1.0 result and the semi-synthetic proof of concept.

3. **"Semi-synthetic injection is artificial"** — We inject into real response matrices (not simulated), preserving real ability distributions and item characteristics. The mechanism (incorrect→correct flipping) is a simplification acknowledged in limitations.

4. **"DIF power is only sufficient for large effects"** — Large effects are precisely what threaten benchmark validity most. Operational region: N≥80, δ≥1.4, TPR=0.68-0.80.

5. **"Only validated on MMLU"** — Partially addressed: GSM8K replication (METABENCH 1,319 items × 6,702 models) confirms semi-synthetic framework portability (ΔTPR=+0.818) and temporal DIF pattern (C%=18.9%). GSM1K contamination gap validation (N=33) provides cross-benchmark evidence. Full generalization to diverse benchmarks remains future work.

6. **"Higher methods (MIMIC, propensity-score) could solve the confounding"** — Acknowledged as future work. We frame our three-attempt negative results as "empirical observation" that motivates these directions, not as impossibility.

7. **"ETS threshold is uncalibrated for LLM populations"** — ✅ RESOLVED (plan_018). C% at {1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5} = {48.9%, 31.3%, 18.3%, 10.2%}. Finding >15% holds at standard thresholds [1.0, 2.0]. At conservative 2.5, still 10.2% (1,278 items). Present as: "finding is robust across standard thresholds; even at the most conservative cutoff, >10% of items show large DIF." Do NOT claim ">15% at all thresholds" — be honest that 2.5 drops below.

8. **"Multiple testing: 12,508 simultaneous tests without correction"** — ✅ RESOLVED (plan_018). BH FDR correction at q=0.05 removes only 3/3,918 ETS C items (31.32%→31.30%). At higher thresholds, BH impact is zero. ETS dual requirement (effect size + significance) provides near-complete implicit protection. Random-split sanity check (C%=0.18%) confirms empirically.

9. **"Only uniform DIF — non-uniform DIF plausible for LLMs"** — Apply SIBTEST or logistic regression DIF to 5-10 representative subjects as robustness check. Show MH results are not missing substantial non-uniform DIF.

10. **"Ranking disruption result is tautological"** — ✅ RESOLVED (plan_020). Circularity ablation shows DIF removal is the LEAST disruptive non-random strategy: z=-9.5 vs accuracy-gap z=-157, discrimination z=-16, variance z=-108. Despite 62.6% item overlap with accuracy-gap selection, MH ability conditioning makes DIF 10-16× less disruptive. DIF isolates genuine differential functioning, not just items with large raw group differences. Tautology refuted.

## Dropped from Original Framing

- **Ensemble (Claim 2 old)**: plan_003a/b/c never executed. Future work.
- **Regeneration (Claim 3 old)**: Bifactor killed by plan_014 pre-check. Dropped entirely.
- **RL robustness**: Theoretically motivated but N=13 insufficient. Limitations disclosure, not claim.
- **Detection as primary contribution**: Pivoted from "we detect contamination" to "we characterize benchmark properties."

+When we say ``Model B outperforms Model A on MMLU,'' we implicitly assume that the benchmark measures the same construct in the same way for both models. This assumption of temporal comparability underpins every cross-generation comparison published on leaderboards and in model reports, yet it is rarely tested. Applying Mantel-Haenszel Differential Item Functioning (MH-DIF) analysis~\citep{holland1988mh} with Educational Testing Service (ETS) severity classification to the METABENCH response matrix~\citep{kipnis2024metabench}, we find that 31\% of MMLU~\citep{hendrycks2021mmlu} items receive ETS Category~C classification ($|\Delta_{\mathrm{MH}}| \geq 1.5$, $p < 0.05$), indicating large shifts in item functioning between models released in 2023 and 2024. This is not statistical noise: a random-split control within the 2023 cohort yields only 0.18\% ETS~C items. The instability persists within every MMLU subject domain, with domain-level C\% ranging from 31\% to 45\% (mean 38.1\%), and item-level regression shows that 92.4\% of this instability is unrelated to aggregate domain-level accuracy gains. Nearly one in three MMLU items behaves differently depending on when the evaluated models were trained. Crucially, this instability does not threaten benchmark validity: Spearman rank correlation between model rankings computed on all items versus stable-only items is $\rho \approx 0.997$. The instability is diagnostic, not destructive; it reveals which capability dimensions shift across model generations rather than rendering MMLU scores unreliable.

A growing body of contamination detection research has produced sophisticated item-level methods, from membership inference approaches such as Min-K\%~\citep{shi2024mink} to performance-based detectors such as ConStat~\citep{dekoninck2024constat}, DVD~\citep{liang2026dvd}, and Self-Critique~\citep{tao2026selfcritique}. These methods validate detection accuracy primarily against web-overlap labels such as those of \citet{li2024contamination}, which classify benchmark items as contaminated based on verbatim or near-verbatim matches in publicly accessible training corpora. Such labels measure \emph{global exposure}: whether an item exists in the data ecosystem that all training pipelines can access. They do not measure \emph{differential item functioning}: whether an item behaves differently across model cohorts that may have had varying degrees of exposure or different training methodologies. \Cref{fig:global_vs_differential} illustrates the distinction. Most MMLU items are globally contaminated in the sense that they exist in web-accessible text, so all model cohorts encounter them and no differential signal arises. The items that function differentially are those where exposure or training methodology changed asymmetrically across cohorts. Validating differential detectors against global-exposure labels therefore conflates two phenomena, and the near-chance enrichment (0.96) between DIF flags and web-overlap labels is the expected outcome of this mismatch.

The persistent non-reduction shifted our research question: from whether DIF detects contamination, to what the persistent 31\% instability reveals about how benchmarks interact with evolving model populations.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	When we say ``Model B outperforms Model A on MMLU,'' we implicitly assume that the benchmark measures the same construct in the same way for both models. This assumption of temporal comparability underpins every cross-generation comparison published on leaderboards and in model reports, yet it is rarely tested. Applying Mantel-Haenszel Differential Item Functioning (MH-DIF) analysis~\citep{holland1988mh} with Educational Testing Service (ETS) severity classification to the METABENCH response matrix~\citep{kipnis2024metabench}, we find that 31\% of MMLU~\citep{hendrycks2021mmlu} items receive ETS Category~C classification ($|\Delta_{\mathrm{MH}}| \geq 1.5$, $p < 0.05$), indicating large shifts in item functioning between models released in 2023 and 2024. This is not statistical noise: a random-split control within the 2023 cohort yields only 0.18\% ETS~C items. The instability persists within every MMLU subject domain, with domain-level C\% ranging from 31\% to 45\% (mean 38.1\%), and item-level regression shows that 92.4\% of this instability is unrelated to aggregate domain-level accuracy gains. Nearly one in three MMLU items behaves differently depending on when the evaluated models were trained. Crucially, this instability does not threaten benchmark validity: Spearman rank correlation between model rankings computed on all items versus stable-only items is $\rho \approx 0.997$. The instability is diagnostic, not destructive; it reveals which capability dimensions shift across model generations rather than rendering MMLU scores unreliable.
5	
6	A growing body of contamination detection research has produced sophisticated item-level methods, from membership inference approaches such as Min-K\%~\citep{shi2024mink} to performance-based detectors such as ConStat~\citep{dekoninck2024constat}, DVD~\citep{liang2026dvd}, and Self-Critique~\citep{tao2026selfcritique}. These methods validate detection accuracy primarily against web-overlap labels such as those of \citet{li2024contamination}, which classify benchmark items as contaminated based on verbatim or near-verbatim matches in publicly accessible training corpora. Such labels measure \emph{global exposure}: whether an item exists in the data ecosystem that all training pipelines can access. They do not measure \emph{differential item functioning}: whether an item behaves differently across model cohorts that may have had varying degrees of exposure or different training methodologies. \Cref{fig:global_vs_differential} illustrates the distinction. Most MMLU items are globally contaminated in the sense that they exist in web-accessible text, so all model cohorts encounter them and no differential signal arises. The items that function differentially are those where exposure or training methodology changed asymmetrically across cohorts. Validating differential detectors against global-exposure labels therefore conflates two phenomena, and the near-chance enrichment (0.96) between DIF flags and web-overlap labels is the expected outcome of this mismatch.
7	
8	\begin{figure}[t]
9	\centering
10	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_1_global_vs_differential.pdf}
11	\caption{Global vs.\ differential contamination, illustrated via Item Characteristic Curves (ICCs). \textbf{Left}: global contamination produces no DIF; both cohorts encounter the item, and their ICCs overlap. \textbf{Right}: differential contamination produces DIF; the focal cohort's ICC shifts because only that cohort was disproportionately exposed during training. The enrichment ratio of $\approx 1.0$ between DIF flags and web-overlap labels is expected because most MMLU items fall into the left category.}
12	\label{fig:global_vs_differential}
13	\end{figure}
14	
15	We apply classical MH-DIF with ETS classification to the full METABENCH response matrix (5,227 models $\times$ 12,508 MMLU items), the largest-scale DIF analysis on LLM benchmarks to date. This psychometric approach complements concurrent work on anchor-item calibration for score comparability~\citep{habba2026growingpains} and addresses the fragility of existing contamination detectors under post-training perturbation~\citep{wang2026fragility}. Semi-synthetic injection experiments confirm that DIF detects differential contamination when present ($\Delta\mathrm{TPR} = {+}0.508$ at exploitation rate $p = 0.5$), and our cross-subject matching protocol eliminates false positive inflation ($\Delta\mathrm{FPR} = 0.000$). Three structural controls (matched-ability quintile analysis, IRT $\theta$-conditioning, and within-subject pre-checks) confirm that the 31\% temporal instability cannot be attributed to methodological artifacts, establishing it as a robust empirical finding about MMLU's measurement properties.
16	
17	MMLU's 12,508 items provide sufficient measurement redundancy that removing nearly a third does not alter rank order. DIF should therefore be understood as a diagnostic lens (which items changed and for which model families) rather than a quality filter (remove bad items to improve the benchmark). Despite aggregate ranking stability, DIF-flagged items concentrate discriminative signal that differentiates model generations: removing DIF items degrades ranking discriminability more than removing an equal number of random items ($z = -8$ to $-49\sigma$ across 21 conditions). Individual model families show distinctive DIF profiles: Phi-3 and Llama-3 gain ${+}700$ to ${+}850$ rank positions under stable-item evaluation, while Mistral-based merges lose $-400$ to $-587$ positions.
18	
19	We do not modify the MH-DIF procedure itself; the contributions are empirical, not algorithmic. Three layers of genuine novelty emerge: (a)~we discover that 31\% temporal instability is robust across thresholds and unrelated to capability improvement, the first large-scale characterization of item-level benchmark stability at 5,227 models; (b)~we expose a fundamental validation methodology gap in the contamination detection literature, showing that web-overlap labels cannot serve as ground truth for item-level differential detectors; and (c)~we provide a reusable semi-synthetic validation framework with cross-subject matching ($\Delta\mathrm{FPR} = 0.000$), confirmed on GSM8K with independent contamination validation through the GSM1K held-out set~\citep{zhang2024gsm1k}. We make the following contributions:
20	
21	\begin{enumerate}
22	\item \textbf{Benchmark temporal comparability} (Claim 1): 31\% of MMLU items are functionally unstable across model generations under ETS~C classification, with the instability persisting within every subject domain (mean C\% $= 38.1\%$) and confirmed non-random by random-split control at 0.18\% (\Cref{sec:temporal}).
23	
24	\item \textbf{Ground truth meta-critique} (Claim 2): Web-overlap contamination labels~\citep{li2024contamination} cannot evaluate item-level differential detectors. The enrichment between DIF flags and web-overlap labels is 0.96 (chance level), exposing a validation methodology gap in the contamination detection literature (\Cref{sec:groundtruth}).
25	
26	\item \textbf{Semi-synthetic validation framework} (Claim 3): Controlled injection with cross-subject matching achieves $\Delta\mathrm{FPR} = 0.000$ while preserving detection power ($\Delta\mathrm{TPR} = {+}0.508$ at $p = 0.5$); cross-benchmark replication on GSM8K confirms generality (\Cref{sec:semisynthetic,sec:gsm8k}).
27	
28	\item \textbf{DIF as diagnostic lens} (Claim 4): DIF-flagged items concentrate discriminative information ($z = -8$ to $-49\sigma$ vs.\ random removal) and anti-correlate with the GSM1K contamination gap ($r = -0.478$, suggestive at $N = 33$), indicating that DIF captures item-level behavioral change distinct from simple memorization (\Cref{sec:downstream,sec:gsm8k}).
29	\end{enumerate}

## 任务
撰写 Related Work 章节（`paper/sections/related_work.tex`）。

## 写作规范（必读）
开始写作前，你必须先 `Read /home/ubuntu/agent-ml-research/skills/global/paper-writing-norms.skill.md`，严格遵守其中的风格规则（禁用 em-dash、-ing 结尾、AI 写作标记、banned transition words）。

## 结构要求（5 个 cluster，~900-1000 words，目标 ≥1.5 ICLR 页）

### Cluster 1: Contamination Detection Methods（~200 words）
覆盖文献：shi2024mink, zhang2024minkpp, dekoninck2024constat, liang2026dvd, tao2026selfcritique, wang2026fragility, golchin2024timetravel, balloccu2024leak, li2024contamination
核心定位：这些方法都用 web-overlap / n-gram 标签做 ground truth 验证——这正是我们 Claim 2 (ground truth meta-critique) 指出的 validation methodology gap。强调：它们检测 global exposure，而 DIF 检测 differential item functioning。两者互补但验证标准不可混用。Wang et al. (2026) 的 RL fragility 发现进一步动机化我们的 psychometric 方法（行为模式 vs NLL 信号）。

### Cluster 2: IRT in LLM Evaluation（~250 words）— 最重要的 cluster
覆盖文献：habba2026growingpains, zhou2026psnirt, lalor2019irt, vania2021irt, hardy2026scalability, li2025atlas, chen2025irtnet, choi2026llmjudgeirt, kim2019fpc, maiapolo2024tinybenchmarks

**必须包含与 Growing Pains (Habba et al. 2026) 的专门技术对比段落**：
- Growing Pains：用固定参数标定 (FPC) + 100 anchor items 实现可扩展评估 (extensible evaluation)，解决 score comparability
- 我们：用 DIF 诊断哪些 items 跨代不稳定，告诉 Growing Pains 哪些 anchor items 正在退化
- 互补关系：their framework + our diagnostic = monitored extensible evaluation
- 引用 habba2026growingpains，引用 kim2019fpc（FPC 方法论）

其他 IRT 工作：Lalor et al. (2019) 开创 IRT-NLP 交叉；Vania et al. (2021) IRT 分析 test set discriminability；Zhou et al. (2026) PSN-IRT 用 4PL 分析 benchmark quality；Hardy et al. (2026) scalability coefficients 作为轻量级 item quality pre-filter；tinyBenchmarks (Maia Polo et al. 2024) 用 IRT 选择代表性子集。

### Cluster 3: DIF Methodology & Measurement Invariance（~200 words）
覆盖文献：holland1988mh, shealy1993sibtest, clauser1998dif, swaminathan1990logistic, zumbo1999handbook, belzak2020smallsample, lord1980irt, raju1988area, teresi2007dif, meredith1993invariance, vandenberg2000invariance, muthen1985mimic, woods2009mimic
核心定位：MH-DIF 是成熟方法（Holland & Thayer 1988），我们不做算法修改。提及替代方法（logistic regression DIF, SIBTEST, Lord's χ², Raju area）以展示方法论意识。DIF 是 item-level measurement invariance test (Meredith 1993, Vandenberg & Lance 2000)。我们的应用上下文是新的——5,227 "examinees"、57-subject 多维能力——但方法本身已建立。承认 impact-vs-DIF confound 是核心挑战。

### Cluster 4: Benchmark Design & Concurrent Work（~200 words）
覆盖文献：hendrycks2021mmlu, kipnis2024metabench, white2025livebench, chiang2024chatbot, mialon2023gaia, li2024latesteval, kiela2021dynabench, liang2023helm
核心定位：我们 psychometrically characterize 现有 benchmarks（MMLU），他们 build new ones（LiveBench, GAIA, Chatbot Arena）或用替代评估范式。METABENCH 提供我们的 response matrix。动态 benchmarks (Dynabench, LatestEval, LiveBench) 回避 contamination 但 lack psychometric equating across versions。

### Cluster 5: LLM Evaluation Methodology（~100 words）
覆盖文献：chang2024survey, burnell2023rethink, wang2024mmlupro, ott2022benchmark
简要：LLM evaluation 的宏观背景——item-level transparency 不足 (Burnell et al. 2023)、benchmark saturation (Ott et al. 2022)。我们的 DIF 分析提供 item-level 诊断工具。
